CCAR-P · Claude Certified Architect: Professional · 63 items · 120 min · pass 720/1000

CCAR-P Crash Course

One volume, every domain, weighted by exam weight. Decision rules, must-memorize numbers, 25 trap patterns, 25 rapid-fire questions. Built to be enough for all 63 items.

7 domains · weighted D3 19% → D7 7%25 trap patterns · 25 rapid-fire questions

How to use this crash course

Start at Rung 0 before the domains: it says what Claude is, what a token is, and what an architect actually does with them. Then read the domains in exam-weight order: D3, D1, D4, D5, D6, D2, D7, heaviest first. Each domain sheet has three parts: the facts in one screen, the "if the stem says X, pick Y" decision rules, and the traps that domain sets. Then come the must-memorize numbers, the 25 trap patterns, and 25 rapid-fire questions. The pre-exam checklist closes the volume.

This is a judgment exam, not a trivia exam. The questions are long scenario stems. Several options are technically true. The credited answer is the one that best satisfies every stated constraint at once. When you are stuck, name the constraint out loud: cost ceiling, latency budget, compliance rule, existing footprint. The answer that respects all of them wins.

Each domain sheet is a ladder. Rungs 1-2 give you the facts and the decision rules in one screen. Rung 3 adds the granular layer: exact numbers, limits, and worked specifics the exam tests. The top rung is the trap list: name every trap cold before you move on.

Exam-day protocol

Read the question line first, then the scenario. The question line tells you what to extract. Budget just under 2 minutes per item: 63 items in 120 minutes. Flag anything that eats 3 minutes and move on. Use the final 10 minutes for flagged items only, and change an answer only when you can name the error. On multiple-response items, judge each option alone: every selection must survive on its own, because there is no partial credit. About a quarter of the exam is multiple-response. One wrong pick sinks the whole item.

Next: Rung 0: what Claude is, and what the exam tests.

Rung 0 · What Claude is, and what the exam tests

Why this comes next.

The crash course assumes nothing and proves everything fast. Start here: what Claude is, and the shape of what the exam actually tests.

Claude is a large language model. It does one thing: given text, it predicts the most likely next chunk of text, over and over, until it decides to stop.

It does not read words. It reads tokens. A token is a chunk of text: a word, part of a word, or punctuation. "Unbelievable" is three tokens: un, believ, able. Roughly four characters make one token.

Everything you send becomes one long sequence of tokens: your instructions, the conversation so far, the documents, the tool definitions. Claude reads the whole sequence, predicts the next token, appends it, and repeats until the answer is complete. There is no other input channel.

Tokens are also the currency. You pay per token in and per token out. Output tokens cost about 5x input tokens. max_tokens caps the reply length. The context window is how many tokens fit in one request. Keep these facts handy: every cost and latency decision on this exam traces back to them.

What you assemble, every time: the model choice, the instructions, the context, and the tools. What Claude adds: the prediction. What the architect adds: the constraints.

One vocabulary item, used in every domain below. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for plugging tools and data into Claude apps: build the integration once, use it from any app. When one capability must be reused across many surfaces, the exam's answer is MCP.

Next: D3 (Integration), the biggest domain at 19%.

D3 · Integration (19%, about 12 items)

Why this domain comes first.

Rung 0 gave you the vocabulary. Now the seven domains, in exam-weight order. D3 comes first because at 19% (about 12 items) it is the single biggest slice of the exam.

The heaviest domain. Expect a dozen questions on how Claude systems connect to the world.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Pick the integration mechanism by reuse and independence. Three mechanisms, three tells. MCP (Model Context Protocol) when one capability must be reused across many surfaces: three product teams needing the same knowledge-search tool is the textbook tell. Direct API or CLI when it is one application, one surface, full control, no reuse need; wrapping a one-off in a protocol layer adds maintenance with no benefit. Agent-to-agent when two systems must reason and fail independently, with distinct responsibility domains.

Capability bloat is the exam's favorite D3 diagnosis. Signs: tool counts far beyond the task, overlapping tool descriptions where two tools plausibly handle one request, broad write permissions granted "just in case", tools that never appear in invocation logs but ship in every request. The fix is always scoping: minimal tool sets per responsibility, oversized agents split into scoped subagents, least privilege on every credential.

Progressive discovery beats monolithic context at scale. Load tool definitions, schemas, and reference data on demand as the agent narrows in. Front-loading everything into every request costs tokens, dilutes attention, and lowers tool-selection accuracy. Monolithic context is acceptable only for small, stable toolsets.

Agents act with the calling user's permissions. The tested anti-pattern is one over-privileged service account shared by all users: it erases per-user boundaries and audit trails. Secrets live in environment variables or secret managers. Credentials in prompts, code, or committed config are automatic wrong answers. Every tool invocation should be attributable: who triggered it, with which permissions, against which resource.

If the stem says Pick
Multiple teams or clients need the same tool MCP server, build once, expose everywhere
One app, one surface, full control Direct API integration, no protocol layer
Two systems must reason and fail independently Agent-to-agent delegation
Tool count far beyond the task, overlapping descriptions Capability bloat: scope tools, split the agent
Agent carries every schema on every request Progressive discovery, load on demand
One shared service account for all users Per-user authorization, restore audit trails
Secret in a prompt, code, or committed config Move to env var or secret manager, always wrong

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

Chunking, matched to data shape. Prose manuals: fixed 512 tokens with 50 overlap (predictable cost and latency). Support tickets: one ticket = one chunk (never split the problem from its fix). API references: one endpoint = one chunk. Contracts with cross-references: section-aware hierarchical (child chunks for precision, parent chunks for the referenced context). Code: function/class level with file-path metadata.

Retrieval is two stages. The fuel is embeddings: your text turned into a list of numbers (a vector), so search can match by meaning instead of keywords. Stage one casts a wide net: dense vector search plus BM25 keyword search in parallel. Dense vector search finds by meaning using those number-lists (it finds "factory reset procedure" for a "how do I reset" query); BM25 is a classic keyword-ranking algorithm that scores exact word matches by rarity (it finds the exact error code ERR_0x4F2A). The two are merged, top 40 to 100.

Metadata filters run first and can remove 90% of the corpus before similarity runs. Stage two reranks the top 40 down to 5 with a cross-encoder, a small scoring model that reads each query-plus-chunk pair and grades how well it fits: typically +10 to 20 points of faithfulness for a few hundred milliseconds. That is the best quality-per-millisecond trade in the pipeline.

Transport fork. stdio: local subprocess on one machine, single user (Claude Code on a laptop). Streamable HTTP: production, many users, TLS, OAuth, load-balanced. SSE (Server-Sent Events, the older one-way streaming format): deprecated legacy path. Remote, multi-user, or production in the stem means Streamable HTTP; single laptop means stdio.

MCP auth. MCP standardizes how OAuth tokens flow, not whether auth happens. The server still authenticates every caller. Delegated OAuth 2.1: scoped tokens per user, validated on every tool call, per-user instant revocation. A token with *:* scope is a finding, not a shortcut.

Tool errors: the instructive-error rule

When a tool fails, the error message must say what went wrong and what Claude should try next. A generic "Tool execution failed" message produces two failure modes: the agent retries the identical call until it hits the turn limit, or it escalates to a human without trying alternatives. The fix is in the tool, not the prompt: specific error text that names the problem and the next step.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def lookup_order(order_id):
    """Look up one order by its ID. Returns a tool-style result dict."""
    # WHY a dict with is_error: the agent loop reads this field to decide
    # whether to retry, try another tool, or escalate. A bare exception
    # gives the model nothing to reason about.
    order = db_get(order_id)  # pretend this hits your order store
    if order is None:
        # WHAT: the lookup found nothing. WHY this shape: it names the exact
        # failure AND the next step, so the agent tries get_customer for a
        # valid ID instead of retrying this call forever or escalating early.
        # BREAKS IF: you return "Tool execution failed". The agent then has
        # no signal: it retries identically until the turn limit, or gives up
        # and escalates without trying the obvious alternative.
        return {
            "is_error": True,
            "message": (
                f"No order found for id '{order_id}'. "
                "It may be mistyped or belong to a different account. "
                "Call get_customer first to confirm the customer, then retry "
                "lookup_order with the corrected id from that result."
            ),
        }
    # Success path: plain data, no error flag. The agent moves on.
    return {"is_error": False, "order": order}

Walkthrough: one failing tool call, step by step

  Agent calls lookup_order("ORD-999")
        |
        v
  Tool runs, finds nothing
        |
        v
  Tool returns is_error=True + instructive message
  ("no order for ORD-999 ... call get_customer first,
   then retry with the corrected id")
        |
        v
  Agent reads the message, understands the cause
        |
        v
  Agent calls get_customer, gets the real id
        |
        v
  Agent retries lookup_order with the corrected id
        |
        v
  Success. No turn-limit burn, no premature escalation.

  Compare: with a generic "Tool execution failed" message, the
  agent has two bad options: retry the same call (burns turns)
  or escalate (bothers a human for a solvable problem).

Top rung: D3 traps. Name them cold

Mega-agent is the trap: an option that piles tools and permissions onto one agent when the scenario shows bloat. Context-stuffing appears here too: "give the agent every schema" as a fix for bad tool selection. Single-framework shows up in auth questions: one shared account for every jurisdiction and user type.

Next: D1 (Solution Design and Architecture), 17%.

D1 · Solution Design & Architecture (17%, about 11 items)

Why this domain comes next.

D3 covered integration: tools, MCP, and APIs. D1 (17%, about 11 items) tests what you build with those integrations: solution design and architecture.

Pattern selection is the most tested judgment on the exam.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Three patterns, one governing principle: start with the simplest pattern that meets the requirement.

Augmented LLM is a single model call enriched with retrieval, tools, or memory. Pick it when one well-scoped call solves the task: lowest cost, lowest latency. Workflow is multiple model calls in a fixed, developer-defined sequence. Pick it when steps are known in advance and predictability or auditability matters: fixed steps give deterministic, traceable behavior that compliance teams can sign off. Agentic is an open-ended loop where the model chooses its own tools and steps. Pick it only when the solution path cannot be enumerated up front and exploration is required. You accept its cost and latency variance only then.

A complete architecture has four parts: input, processing, output, and a feedback loop. An answer that omits the feedback loop (evals, user signals, monitoring feeding back into design) describes an incomplete system, and the exam notices.

Decompose multi-agent systems only when the decomposition is real. Independent subtasks that can run in parallel justify an orchestrator with workers. A narrow single-domain task belongs to one agent. Decompose by capability (research, analysis, writing) or by data domain (per region, per product line). Sequential handoff when outputs chain; parallel fan-out when subtasks are independent, merged by the orchestrator in a synthesis step. Orchestration lives outside any single agent: the coordinator owns assignment, merging, and failure isolation.

Anchor every recommendation to the named business pillar: efficiency (throughput, automation rate), cost (per-transaction spend), or performance SLAs (latency, availability, accuracy floors). When two answers are technically valid, the one satisfying the stated constraint wins.

If the stem says Pick
Fixed steps, known in advance Workflow
Fixed output structure plus audit trail (per-step logs) Workflow, one call per step, logged
Solution path cannot be listed up front, needs exploration Agentic loop
One well-scoped question, retrieval or one tool call Augmented LLM, the cheapest correct answer
Predictability or compliance sign-off required Workflow, never agentic
"Add autonomy" with no stated reason Reject: agentic-by-default is a defect
Architecture missing evals, monitoring, user feedback Incomplete: add the feedback loop
Subtasks are independent and parallelizable Orchestrator plus workers, merge in synthesis
One narrow task, one data domain One agent, refuse decomposition
Two valid designs, one respects the cost ceiling The cheaper one, constraint-first

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

The trilemma decision procedure, in order:

  1. Read the constraints. "p95 under 2 seconds" pins you near latency (p95 is the 95th percentile: 95 of 100 requests finish faster than this); "95% accuracy on contracts" pins you near quality; "$0.01 per request" pins you near cost.
  2. Rank them and find the binding one. Then pick the cheapest tier that satisfies the binding constraint.
  3. Cheat the triangle with architecture: cache stable prefixes, route the easy majority to the fast tier and escalate only the hard slice, batch everything without a latency requirement (Batch API is ~50% off).
  4. Discipline the output. Output tokens cost ~5x input, so one-sentence answers and JSON instead of prose cut the most expensive tokens first.

Multi-agent triggers. One agent reading 50 sources sequentially fills its context with raw articles and gets worse as the run goes on. The fix: orchestrator-workers for independent parallel research (each worker gets its own context with 5 articles and one narrow job), then a sequential verify step, then evaluator-optimizer for the writing (draft, critique against a rubric, revise once). Context isolation is the named quality mechanism: 150,000 raw tokens compress to ~15,000 tokens of structured summaries.

Match independence to topology: independent parallel = orchestrator-workers; needs judging = evaluator-optimizer; output chains = sequential pipeline; recursive decomposition = hierarchy. Mesh for independent tasks is the coordination-overhead trap.

Routing math. At 50,000 queries a day with the fast tier nailing 85%: triage on the cheap tier, escalate only the hard 15%. Upgrading everything pays flagship prices for already-solved traffic.

Routing: the pattern behind "routing beats a single model at scale"

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def answer(query: str) -> str:
    # WHY route at all: the fast tier handles the easy majority at a
    # fraction of the price. Only the hard slice pays flagship rates.
    # On the exam this beats "upgrade everything" every single time.

    # Step 1: triage with the cheap, fast tier. max_tokens=16 keeps the
    # classification call tiny: we need one word back, not an essay.
    # BREAKS IF: you use the flagship tier here. Triage runs on every
    # request, so an expensive triage erases the savings routing exists for.
    triage = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5",
        max_tokens=16,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Classify as SIMPLE or COMPLEX:\n{query}",
        }],
    ).content[0].text.strip()

    # Step 2: pick the tier from the triage verdict. Simple stays cheap;
    # complex escalates to the balanced tier. The default is the cheap
    # tier, so an unclear verdict fails safe toward low cost.
    model = (
        "claude-haiku-4-5" if triage == "SIMPLE"
        else "claude-sonnet-4-6"
    )

    # Step 3: answer with the chosen tier. One call, no loop, no agent.
    # WHY not agentic here: the path is fully determined by the triage
    # result. Autonomy with no open question is the agentic-by-default trap.
    return client.messages.create(
        model=model,
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": query}],
    ).content[0].text

Walkthrough: one query through the router, step by step

  User query arrives
        |
        v
  Triage call (Haiku, 16 tokens out): "SIMPLE" or "COMPLEX"
        |
        +---> SIMPLE --> answer with Haiku (cheap, fast)
        |
        +---> COMPLEX -> answer with Sonnet (capable, pricier)
        |
        v
  Single response returned. Total: 2 model calls, cheapest
  tier that can handle the query.

  Data in: raw query. What happens: 1-word classification, then
  tier selection. Data out: answer at the lowest sufficient cost.

Top rung: D1 traps. Name them cold

Agentic-by-default: any option that adds an autonomous loop where a workflow or single call suffices. Flagship-everywhere: upgrading all traffic to the top tier when routing solves it. Skip-discovery: an architecture answer that jumps to design with no success metrics or constraints named.

Next: D4 (Evaluation, Testing and Optimization), 16%.

D4 · Evaluation, Testing & Optimization (16%, about 10 items)

Why this domain comes next.

You can design it and connect it. D4 (16%, about 10 items) asks the next question: how do you know it works, and how do you make it better?

Diagnosis questions: given symptoms, name the failure and the fix.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Match the symptom to the failure before touching anything. Wrong documents retrieved means a retrieval failure: fix chunking, embeddings, or query construction, and consider re-ranking. Right documents but wrong or invented answers means a generation failure: check grounding, prompts, or the model tier. Fast tier failing only on hard slices means a tier mismatch: route, do not upgrade everything. Judge scores drifting from human perception means judge miscalibration: sample, compare against human review, recalibrate the rubric.

Design eval sets like production, then maintain them. Held-out (never used for tuning), shaped like real traffic, refreshed as traffic drifts, scored per slice. An eval set frozen at launch measures the past: the score stays high because the test stayed easy. Tuning prompts on the test set is cheating yourself; the exam marks it wrong every time.

Divide grading labor by what each grader is good at. Deterministic checks (does the JSON parse, do the fields match the schema) go to code. Fuzzy quality judgments at scale go to an LLM judge, calibrated against sampled human review. Final calls on high-stakes or ambiguous cases go to humans. When judge scores and human perception diverge, the rubric no longer matches human standards: recalibrate.

Run one clean experiment at a time. Change one variable, hold the rest, measure against the held-out set. Multi-variable experiments prove nothing. "Feels better" rollouts are not evidence.

If the stem says Pick
Top retrieved chunks are off-topic Retrieval failure: fix chunking, embeddings, query; consider re-ranking
Team proposes retrieving more chunks to fix bad chunks Reject: context-stuffing, more noise, more cost
Right docs in, wrong answers out Generation failure: grounding, prompt, or tier
Fast tier fine on easy, fails on hard slice Tier mismatch: route the hard slice up
Judge scores rise while complaints rise Judge miscalibration: sample, compare, recalibrate
Eval set built at launch, never refreshed, traffic drifted Eval decay: refresh the set, add new formats as a scored slice
"Tune the prompt until the test set looks good" Reject: tuning on the test set
Two changes shipped together, metrics moved Reject: one variable per experiment
One number for the whole system Reject: aggregate-metric, score per slice
High recall, low precision in first-stage retrieval Add a re-ranker before the prompt
Exact identifiers: error codes, SKUs Hybrid keyword-plus-semantic search
Corpus partitions cleanly by product, region, date Metadata filter before semantic search

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

Golden sets. 200 to 500 real, held-out cases with known-good answers, versioned in git, covering every document type and the hard query shapes (multi-hop, ambiguous, unanswerable). Built from production inputs, refreshed as traffic drifts. Fewer than 100 and noise dominates: a 3-point swing might be two lucky cases.

CI gate rules, concrete. Accuracy floor (e.g. 90% faithfulness). Per-segment: no document type, tool, or category may drop more than ~2 points from the previous run, even if the overall score holds. Latency ceiling (p95 under the SLA). Cost ceiling (mean tokens per task within budget). Safety: a dedicated adversarial slice passes at 100%, binary, never averaged. The gate posts a score diff as a PR comment and blocks merge on any red rule.

Judge calibration. An LLM judge without a rubric and human-agreement calibration is an opinion with a score attached. Rubric with named criteria and point values ("2 points: cites the correct section; 1 point: correct but uncited; 0: contradicts the reference"). Calibrate: humans score 100 outputs, judge scores the same 100, measure agreement (trust needs roughly 85%+). Know the biases: judges favor longer answers, confident tone, and their own model family's style.

Monitoring in production. Sample ~5% of live traffic, score nightly, track the trend: a slow 1-point-per-week decay is data drift, invisible without the trend line. Alert on judge-score drops, refusal-rate spikes, tool-error spikes, p95 breaching SLA, cost-per-task jumps. Every production failure the golden set missed becomes a new golden case.

Top rung: D4 traps. Name them cold

Aggregate-metric: the single overall accuracy number hiding a per-slice failure. Context-stuffing: "retrieve more chunks" as a quality fix. Prompt-guarantee: tuning the prompt to fix a retrieval or tier problem.

Next: D5 (Governance, Safety and Risk Management), 14%.

D5 · Governance, Safety & Risk Management (14%, about 9 items)

Why this domain comes next.

A system that works still needs to be safe. D5 (14%, about 9 items): governance, safety, and risk management.

Defense in depth, human placement, and matching the framework to the jurisdiction.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Five guardrail layers, in order, each catching what the others miss:

  1. Input filtering scans the request before it reaches the model: injection detectors, PII redaction, jailbreak patterns, rate limits.
  2. Classifier gates score input and output with a small fast model: toxicity, self-harm, disallowed advice; probabilistic, so you set a threshold.
  3. Policy engines are deterministic rules evaluated like code: block SSN patterns, refuse deny-list topics, require approval before writes; no prompt can negotiate with them.
  4. Output filtering scans the response: PII and secret leaks, hallucinations checked against retrieved sources, toxicity re-screen, structured-output validation.
  5. Tool-use controls govern agents: least-privilege scopes, argument allow-lists, human confirmation before irreversible actions, sandboxed code execution.

Attack in the request means input-side controls. Failure in the response means output-side controls. An input filter cannot catch a hallucination; an output filter cannot stop an injection. Compliance and safety enforcement come from permissions, validation, and layers, never from prompt text alone: "tune the system prompt to be safe" is the prompt-guarantee trap.

Place humans by risk, sample the rest. This is human-in-the-loop (HITL): a human reviews before the system acts. Human review is required before irreversible or regulated decisions reach anyone: loan approvals, medical guidance, money movement, data sent outside the company. Routine low-risk steps get sampled review, not review of everything: reviewing every internal draft is the all-or-nothing HITL trap in the other direction. Sentiment and self-reported model confidence are not triggers for human review.

Match the framework to the data and the jurisdiction, sometimes several at once. GDPR governs personal data of people in the EU. HIPAA governs US health data, and it demands a signed BAA (business associate agreement) with any processor. FedRAMP governs US federal cloud deployments. "Encrypt everything" is not a compliance answer: encryption is not a BAA, an audit trail, or a data protection impact assessment (DPIA).

If the stem says Pick
Users pasting "ignore all previous instructions" Input-side injection and jailbreak detection
Answers leaking another customer's data Output-side PII and secret-leak filtering
A rule that must never bend (block SSNs, deny-list topic) Policy engine, deterministic, not a prompt
Agent about to send, delete, or pay Tool-use controls plus human confirmation
"Make the system safe" as the whole answer Reject: residual risk always remains; name monitoring and accepted risk
Loan approval, medical advice, money movement Human review before it reaches anyone
Routine drafts, low-risk summaries Sampled review, not review of everything
EU users' personal data GDPR
US patient data, vendor processing it HIPAA plus a signed BAA
US federal agency deployment FedRAMP
"Encrypt everything" for a compliance question Reject: encryption is not a BAA, audit trail, or DPIA
"The model is aligned" as the safety plan Reject: alignment is not a system control

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

HITL tiers, exact. Read-only: no approval, just log. Reversible writes (file a ticket, update status): no approval, but show what was done and offer undo. Destructive or sensitive (reset password, restart production, delete data, touch another employee's records): explicit human approval with the full action previewed; approvals expire (~5 minutes); timeout defaults to deny, never to allow. Irreversible or regulated (terminate an account, wipe a device): approval plus a second factor, a different human or a manager role. The agent proposes; it never executes alone.

Zero Data Retention, precisely. ZDR is a contract covering the vendor's API: the provider stores none of your request or response data after serving it. It does not cover your laptop: local transcripts, shell history, and your own logs may still hold pasted secrets. A leaked credential gets rotated even under ZDR, and you add a PreToolUse hook (deterministic code that inspects every tool call before it runs and can veto it) that blocks secret-shaped input before it reaches the model. Rule stands regardless of contract: reference secrets by name, never by value.

Fairness is measured, not prompted. "Be fair" in the system prompt is the prompt-guarantee trap. The credited answer: per-slice evaluation across demographic groups, with the slices named and the gaps quantified. Sentiment and self-reported model confidence are not triggers for human review; irreversible impact is.

Top rung: D5 traps. Name them cold

Prompt-guarantee: a system prompt offered as a compliance or safety control. All-or-nothing HITL: humans on everything or humans on nothing. Single-framework: one framework named for data that needs two, or the wrong framework for the jurisdiction.

Next: D6 (Stakeholder Communication and Lifecycle), 14%.

D6 · Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle (14%, about 9 items)

Why this domain comes next.

Safe systems still fail without ownership and communication. D6 (14%, about 9 items): stakeholder communication and lifecycle.

The exam spends real weight on work that never touches code. Technically strong candidates lose points here.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Never design before discovery. Structured discovery fills five buckets before any architecture is drawn. Success metrics: numbers with dates. Constraints: latency caps, cost ceilings, compliance rules. Data reality: what data exists, who owns it, how fresh it is. Risk tolerance: what a wrong answer costs, which sets the human review budget. Decision rights: named people who sign off. A scenario that jumps to design with none of these is the skip-discovery trap. Stakeholders describe solutions, not problems: "we want RAG" is a solution; "analysts cannot find the right policy document" is a problem. Dig for the problem.

The lifecycle has six phases: discover, design, build, hand off, monitor, iterate. Then the loop turns again. The steering wheel for the whole loop is the eval set: every iteration is judged by measured results, not opinions. Handoff needs runbooks and baselines, or operations inherits a black box.

Write SLAs for probabilistic systems with error budgets, not deterministic promises. "99.9% correct" is a lie for a model; "95% of responses meet the quality bar, measured weekly on the held-out set, with rollback if we miss two weeks running" is a commitment you can keep. Convert model behavior into commitments the business can plan around.

Preserve reasoning in architecture decision records. An ADR captures context, the options considered, the decision, and the consequences, version controlled with the project. When compliance asks how the team will preserve the reasoning behind a choice, the answer is the ADR. A code comment captures what, rarely why-not-alternatives. A recorded meeting is unsearchable and unversioned. The system prompt encodes behavior, not reasoning.

If the stem says Pick
"Isn't what we needed", no success criteria written Discovery failed: the five buckets were never filled
Stakeholder asks for RAG by name Dig for the problem underneath the named solution
How to preserve why a pattern was chosen ADR: context, options, decision, consequences, versioned
Promise about model behavior Error budget and measured quality bar, never "always correct"
Handoff with no runbooks or baselines Incomplete handoff, operations gets a black box
Which phase does this problem belong to Map it: discover, design, build, hand off, monitor, iterate
"The team" as decision maker Reject: name the person who signs off

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

The five discovery buckets, verbatim-ready. Success metrics: numbers with dates ("analysts find the right policy in under 2 minutes, measured by next quarter"). Constraints: latency caps, cost ceilings, compliance rules. Data reality: what data exists, who owns it, how fresh it is. Risk tolerance: what a wrong answer costs, which sets the human review budget. Decision rights: named people who sign off. A scenario with none of these is skip-discovery, even if the architecture looks beautiful.

SLA anatomy for probabilistic systems. Four pieces: the quality bar ("95% of responses meet the rubric"), the measurement ("scored weekly on the held-out set"), the consequence ("rollback if we miss two weeks running"), and the error budget (how many misses the quarter tolerates). Never "99.9% correct."

ADR anatomy. Context (what was true when we decided), options considered (at least two, with the rejected ones named), the decision, and the consequences. Version controlled with the project. A code comment captures what, rarely why-not-alternatives; a recorded meeting is unsearchable and unversioned.

Trade-off communication. Frame every recommendation by the binding constraint: "Option A meets the latency budget but costs 3x; Option B meets the budget but needs sampled review on edge cases." The feasibility verdict must include "no": recommending against the build, with the constraint it would break, is a complete answer.

Top rung: D6 traps. Name them cold

Skip-discovery: designing from a wish list. Deterministic-correctness promises: "the model will always" anything. The ADR question is nearly verbatim on the exam: learn its phrasing.

Next: D2 (Models, Prompting and Context), 13%.

D2 · Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering (13%, about 8 items)

Why this domain comes next.

D6 closed the lifecycle loop. D2 (13%, about 8 items) returns to the foundation the other domains assume: models, prompting, and context. Lightly tested, but the traps here are expensive.

Tier judgment, caching mechanics, and prompt structure.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Reason by tier, not by model name. Top capability tier (Opus class): hardest reasoning, long-horizon agentic work, where failure is expensive and volume is low. Balanced tier (Sonnet class): the production default for most enterprise workloads. Fast tier (Haiku class): lowest cost and latency, for high-volume well-bounded tasks like classification, routing, extraction. Three rules. Default to the balanced tier and move on evidence: upgrade when evals show reasoning failures, downgrade when the cheap tier holds accuracy. Routing beats a single model at scale. Latency-sensitive user paths get the fast tier plus streaming, while bulk work goes to the Batch API.

Prompting techniques by task shape. Zero-shot (instructions only) for simple, unambiguous tasks. Few-shot with 2 to 4 worked examples to teach format and edge-case judgment; include a correct rejection example so the model learns what to leave alone. Chain-of-thought for multi-step logic, at the price of output tokens and latency. System prompt order: role first, explicit testable criteria next, boundary statements, then output format. "Flag SQL injection and authentication bypass" is testable; "be careful" is not.

Prompt caching pays off when a long, stable prefix is reused across many calls within the cache lifetime. Agent loops, high-traffic endpoints sharing one system prompt, repeated Q&A over the same documents. It breaks on any prefix change from that point forward. The three classic cache-breaking mistakes, all tested: a timestamp or user ID placed early in the system prompt, reordered tool definitions between calls, shuffled document order. Structure prompts stable-first, variable-last, with per-request content after the cache breakpoint. It does not pay off for infrequent calls (the cache expires between them) or prompts below the minimum cacheable length.

Attention concentrates at the edges of the context window. Put critical instructions and key facts at the beginning and end; long middles get skimmed. Trim tool outputs to the fields the next step needs.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

# Stable content first, volatile content last. Everything before the
# cache_control checkpoint is processed once and reused across calls.
# Everything after it is processed fresh on every request.
POLICIES = open("policies.txt").read()        # stable: same for all traffic
OUTPUT_FORMAT = open("format.txt").read()     # stable: same for all traffic

def ask(per_request: str) -> str:
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=[
            {
                "type": "text",
                # WHY one block: a single stable prefix maximizes the
                # cached region. Splitting stable text into many blocks
                # with separate checkpoints wastes breakpoints.
                "text": POLICIES + OUTPUT_FORMAT,
                # The checkpoint. Cached reads cost a fraction of base
                # input price; the write costs a small premium once per
                # cache lifetime. BREAKS IF: you put per_request text
                # before this line. Any change above the checkpoint
                # invalidates everything below it on every single call.
                "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
            }
        ],
        # Volatile content lives AFTER the checkpoint, in messages.
        # Timestamps, user IDs, and session data belong here, never
        # at the top of the system prompt.
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": per_request}],
    ).content[0].text

Walkthrough: two requests through the cached prompt

  Request 1: system=[POLICIES+FORMAT checkpoint] + "Q1"
        |
        v
  Cache WRITE: prefix processed once (small premium),
  stored for the cache lifetime (5 min default)
        |
        v
  Request 2: system=[same prefix checkpoint] + "Q2"
        |
        v
  Cache READ: prefix reused at a steep discount, only
  "Q2" is processed fresh
        |
        v
  Both answers correct, second call much cheaper.

  Data in: stable prefix + per-request question. What happens:
  prefix hashed once, matched on later calls. Data out:
  answer with the prefix billed at read rates, not full price.
If the stem says Pick
High volume, well-bounded (classify, route, extract) Fast tier
Production default, most enterprise workloads Balanced tier
Failure is expensive, volume is low, hard reasoning Top capability tier
Fast tier handles 85%, fails on hard multi-policy slice Route: fast triages, hard slice escalates
Cache hit rate near zero, timestamp at top of prompt Move volatile fields below the breakpoint
"Raise the TTL" or "add more breakpoints" for low hits Reject: check prefix stability first
Teach format and edge-case judgment Few-shot, 2 to 4 examples, include a rejection example
Multi-step logic Chain-of-thought, accept the token cost
Vague criteria like "be careful" Rewrite as testable criteria
Critical instruction buried mid-prompt Move to the edges of the window

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

Breakpoint ordering. Stable-first, variable-last, one breakpoint per stability tier. [1] system prompt + persona + global rules (almost never changes). [2] tool definitions + few-shot examples (changes on deploy). [3] retrieved documents or conversation summary (changes per session). Then the user's current message with no cache (changes every turn). Tool definitions are ideal cache citizens: long, identical across turns, and exactly what capability bloat makes expensive. Never put timestamps, request IDs, or user-specific data inside the cached prefix. With 4 breakpoints max, a fifth explicit breakpoint returns a 400 error.

The break-even math.

cache write = 1.25 × base input price (a 25% premium, paid once per TTL window)
cache read = 0.1 × base input price (90% off the cached portion, paid per hit)

where: base input price = the model’s normal input price per million tokens; TTL = 5 minutes by default.

Worked example: the first write repays itself.

Sonnet 5 charges $2 per million input tokens. Take a 1,000-token prefix and 50 requests inside one 5-minute TTL. No cache: 50 × 1,000 × $2/1M = $0.10.

Cached: one write at 1,000 × $2.50/1M = $0.0025, plus 50 reads at 1,000 × $0.20/1M = $0.01. Total $0.0125. The write is repaid after the very first cache hit.

When the bet loses: 1 request per hour against a 5-minute TTL means every request pays the $0.0025 write and never gets a read, 25% more than no caching.

The 1-hour TTL option keeps entries alive longer but its write costs ~2x base input: only wins when reuse is spread thin across the hour. Reuse interval must be comfortably shorter than the TTL, and the prefix must clear the model-specific minimum (512 / 1024 / 2048 / 4096 tokens).

Model tier pricing. Fable 5.1 $10/$50 per million in/out: hardest reasoning, long-horizon agentic work, last resort. Opus 5.5 $4/$20: sustained agentic coding and knowledge work. Sonnet 5 $2/$10: the balanced production default. Haiku 4.5 $1/$5: high-volume, well-bounded tasks (classification, extraction, routing, subagent workers). Ratios to memorize: output costs exactly 5x input on every tier; each tier costs roughly 1.7x to 5x the one below. Uniform tiering is the expensive distractor.

Top rung: D2 traps. Name them cold

Flagship-everywhere: top tier for traffic the fast tier already handles. Cache-breaker blindness: any fix that ignores the volatile prefix. Vague criteria: untestable instructions presented as a solution.

Next: D7 (Developer Productivity and Enablement), 7%.

D7 · Developer Productivity & Enablement (7%, about 4 items)

Why this domain comes last.

Last domain, smallest slice (7%, about 4 items): developer productivity and enablement. Mechanical questions, easy marks if you know the layer rule.

Small domain, mechanical questions. Team behavior lives in version-controlled project config.

Rungs 1-2: the facts in one screen

Put team-wide behavior in committed project configuration. Shared MCP servers, coding standards, review conventions: they live in the project's version-controlled config (committed CLAUDE.md, project-scoped MCP config with secrets in environment variables), not in each engineer's personal config, not in a wiki nobody's tooling reads. Depending on every individual to comply forever is not a control.

Enforcement and guidance live in different layers. Managed settings enforce: permission deny rules, blocked tools, sandbox requirements. The client enforces them regardless of what the model decides. Managed CLAUDE.md guides: coding standards, compliance reminders, behavioral prose. An enterprise scenario asking how to prevent an action across every machine wants managed settings. One asking how to standardize behavior wants the managed CLAUDE.md. Putting a hard requirement in the soft layer (or prose standards in the enforcement layer) is the trap.

Least privilege in shared and CI environments. Shared checkouts and CI runners get the minimum tool set and the minimum permissions that do the job. Raw secrets never appear in committed files.

If the stem says Pick
Same review conventions for every engineer Version-controlled project config, committed CLAUDE.md
"No session may ever call external network tools, every repo, every machine" Managed settings, permission deny rules (enforced by the client)
"Apply company coding standards everywhere" Managed CLAUDE.md (guidance, not enforcement)
Ban in personal config, standards in personal CLAUDE.md Reject: individuals cannot be the control plane
Secrets for shared MCP servers Environment variables, never committed raw
Shared or CI environment with broad permissions Least privilege: minimum tools, minimum permissions

Rung 3: the granular layer (numbers and limits)

Three settings layers, one rule: lower layers cannot be overridden by higher ones. Managed (enterprise) settings: the org's non-overridable policy (deny rules, blocked tools). Project settings: checked into the repo, team convention (shared MCP servers, project hooks). User settings: personal defaults. Permissions merge across layers with deny-first: a managed deny on git push --force survives any local edit. Compliance or "cannot be overridden" in the stem means managed.

Allow / ask / deny. Allow: run silently. Ask: pause for human approval. Deny: block and log. Ask is a speed bump, not a control: developers under deadline click through prompts, so ask slows accidents without preventing them. Deny is the only hard control. When the scenario demands a guarantee ("must never", "compliance requires"), ask is the trap and deny is the answer.

Hooks. PreToolUse hooks inspect every tool call before execution and can veto it: secret-shaped input never reaches the model, destructive patterns get blocked regardless of what the prompt says. PostToolUse hooks can log or transform results. Hooks are deterministic code, so unlike prompt rules they cannot be talked around.

Debugging production systems. Traces are the core dump: system prompt, every message, every tool_use with exact input, every tool_result, stop_reason per step, token counts, latencies, one correlation ID per session. Debug order: stop reasons first (cut-off behavior), then tool_use/tool_result pairs (wrong actions), then tool schema change history (intermittent wrong-tool calls = schema drift). Reproducing a bug requires frozen replay with canned tool results: re-running the prompt alone proves nothing, because temperature, model version, schemas, and tool results are all inputs.

Runbooks. Mitigate first, diagnose second, harden third. Spend spike at 2am: kill the sessions and enforce an iteration cap, then read the traces; the hardening change (iteration caps, idempotent tools, spend limits) is the lasting fix. A runbook is time-buying; the fix is the code change.

Top rung: D7 traps. Name them cold

Personal-config trap: team standards placed where only one person sees them. Layer confusion: enforcement in the guidance layer or guidance in the enforcement layer.

The 25 trap patterns

Why this comes next.

Numbers memorized. Now the traps: 25 patterns the exam reuses across domains, named so you can spot them inside the options.

Professional distractors are plausible and technically true in some context. Each pattern below marks an option wrong for the scenario at hand. On multiple-response items, apply them per option: one trapped pick sinks the item.

# Trap What it looks like Why it fails
1 Flagship-everywhere Top tier for all traffic Ignores cost and latency; tier must match difficulty and volume
2 Agentic-by-default Autonomous loop with no open question Autonomy without a reason is a defect; simplest sufficient pattern wins
3 Prompt-guarantee "Tune the system prompt" for safety or compliance Enforcement comes from permissions, validation, layers; prompts can be talked around
4 Context-stuffing More context, more chunks, more schemas as the fix Precision and structure are the levers, not volume
5 Mega-agent One agent with every tool and permission Bloat degrades tool selection and widens the blast radius
6 Skip-discovery Design answers with no metrics, constraints, or access Architect answers establish those first
7 All-or-nothing HITL Humans on everything, or humans on nothing Placement is risk-based: humans on irreversible and regulated, sampling on routine
8 Aggregate-metric One overall accuracy number Stratified per-slice evaluation is the professional answer
9 Single-framework One framework for every jurisdiction Framework must match data type and jurisdiction, sometimes several at once
10 Retrieve-more-chunks Raising 5 chunks to 20 to fix bad chunks More noise, more cost; fix chunking, embeddings, query first
11 Tune-on-the-test-set "Tune until the eval set looks good" A tuned-on test set measures nothing; keep evals held out
12 Shared-service-account One privileged account for all users Erases per-user boundaries and audit trails
13 Timestamp-in-prefix Volatile fields at the top of a cached prompt Every request invalidates the cache from position zero
14 Raise-the-TTL Longer TTL as the fix for low cache hits Hit rate is about prefix stability, not lifetime
15 Deterministic-promises "The model will always be correct" Probabilistic systems get error budgets, not guarantees
16 Comments-instead-of-ADR A code comment as the preserved reasoning Comments capture what, rarely why-not-alternatives; ADRs are versioned
17 Wiki-instead-of-config Conventions in a wiki page Invisible to tooling; team behavior lives in committed project config
18 Few-shot-for-capability-gap More examples to fix hard reasoning failures Prompting fixes do not close capability gaps; route or upgrade
19 Upgrade-before-routing Move all traffic up a tier Routing captures cheap easy traffic and quality hard traffic
20 Sample-for-irreversible "Sample 2%" on loan approvals or money movement Sampling measures; it does not prevent. Irreversible means human review
21 Encrypt-everything Encryption as the compliance answer Encryption is not a BAA, an audit trail, or a DPIA
22 Model-is-aligned Alignment as the safety plan Alignment is not a system control; layers are
23 Vague-criteria "Be careful", "be fair" as instructions Untestable; rewrite as testable criteria
24 Missing-feedback-loop Architecture with no evals or monitoring feeding back Incomplete system; the loop is the fourth part
25 Protocol-on-one-off MCP or agent machinery for a single-surface integration Maintenance with no benefit; direct API suffices

25 rapid-fire questions

Why this comes next.

Traps named. Now speed: 25 questions to answer fast, proving recall under pressure.

Tap each question for the answer and the one-line why. Cover your screen, answer out loud, then check.

Q1 (D3). Three product teams want the same knowledge-search capability in Claude Code, a desktop assistant, and a customer-facing agent. Mechanism?

B: one MCP server. Build once, expose everywhere across surfaces is MCP's defining tell. Three direct integrations triple maintenance.

Q2 (D3). A claims-triage agent grew from 6 tools to 34. Accuracy fell 91% to 78%, tool-selection latency rose 2.3s. Two findings justify decomposition first?

Overlapping tool descriptions across claim categories, and the 34 tools serving four distinct workflow domains. Both prove the agent is several agents wearing one coat; a router on top adds a call without fixing bloat.

Q3 (D3). Every engineer shares one service account for agent tool calls. What breaks?

Per-user authorization and audit trails. The fix is per-user permissions so every invocation is attributable to a person.

Q4 (D3). An agent loads all 40 tool schemas on every request. Tool selection is getting worse as tools are added. Fix?

Progressive discovery: load definitions on demand as the agent narrows in. Monolithic context dilutes attention and inflates cost.

Q5 (D3). A tool returns 'Tool execution failed' and the agent either retries identically to the turn limit or escalates immediately. Root cause?

The error message is generic. Instructive errors name what went wrong and what to try next; the fix is in the tool, not the prompt.

Q6 (D1). A legal team needs contracts summarized into a fixed five-section brief, every time, with an auditable trail. Pattern?

Workflow: one model call per section, inputs and outputs logged. Fixed structure plus auditability is the workflow tell; agentic adds forbidden autonomy.

Q7 (D1). A batch job follows fixed steps: extract metadata, classify, summarize, persist. Pattern?

Workflow. Steps are known in advance and never change; there is nothing to explore, so an agent loop is the agentic-by-default trap.

Q8 (D1). A support assistant handles 50,000 queries daily. The fast tier nails 85% but fails complex multi-policy questions. Move?

Route: fast tier triages and handles routine traffic, escalating the hard slice. Upgrading everything pays flagship prices for solved traffic.

Q9 (D1). An architecture diagram shows input, processing, and output but no evals, monitoring, or user feedback. Verdict?

Incomplete architecture. The feedback loop is the fourth part; without it the system cannot learn from production.

Q10 (D4). RAG answers are frequently wrong. Traces show the top retrieved chunks are usually off-topic. The team proposes 5 to 20 chunks. Assessment?

Wrong. Retrieval precision is the problem, so more chunks add more noise and cost. Fix chunking, embeddings, or query construction, and consider re-ranking.

Q11 (D4). Two months post-launch, judge scores drift upward while customer complaints rise. What broke?

Judge calibration. The rubric no longer matches human quality standards; sample outputs, compare against human review, recalibrate.

Q12 (D4). Weekly evals score 97%, but one region reports rising errors. The eval set was built at launch and never refreshed while regional formats changed. What failed?

Eval dataset maintenance. The frozen set measures the past; refresh it and add the new formats as a scored slice.

Q13 (D4). A team ships a new prompt and a new model tier together, and metrics move. Can they claim the prompt helped?

No. Two variables changed at once; run one clean experiment per variable against the held-out set.

Q14 (D5). Users paste 'ignore all previous instructions' into a customer chatbot. Which guardrail layer answers?

Input filtering: injection and jailbreak detection on the request path. An output filter cannot stop an injection.

Q15 (D5). An underwriting assistant recommends loan approvals. Which two controls are required? (Select TWO)

Human review before any final approval reaches a customer, and per-slice evaluation across demographic groups. Irreversible regulated decisions demand HITL; fairness demands stratified evals. A "be fair" system prompt is the prompt-guarantee trap.

Q16 (D5). A vendor will process US patient records through the system. What must the contract include?

A signed BAA under HIPAA. Encryption alone is not a compliance answer.

Q17 (D6). A pilot 'works' but stakeholders say it is not what they needed. No written success criteria, no constraint inventory, no baseline exist. Which phase failed?

Discovery. All three missing artifacts are discovery outputs; a working system missing the need is exactly what skipped discovery produces.

Q18 (D6). Compliance asks how the team will preserve the reasoning behind choosing workflow over agentic, for future maintainers. Answer?

An ADR: context, options, decision, consequences, version controlled with the project. Comments capture what, not why-not-alternatives.

Q19 (D6). The business wants a commitment on answer quality. Which SLA is credible?

An error budget: 95% of responses meet the quality bar measured weekly on the held-out set, with rollback after two misses. Never promise deterministic correctness from a probabilistic system.

Q20 (D2). An agent's prompt starts with the current timestamp, then system prompt, tools, and documents. Caching saves almost nothing. Why?

The timestamp changes every request, invalidating the cached prefix from position zero. Move volatile fields below the breakpoint; stable-first, variable-last.

Q21 (D2). A prompt is 400 tokens, fully stable, called twice a day. Why does caching not help?

Two misses at once: below the minimum cacheable length for most tiers, and too infrequent, so the cache expires between calls.

Q22 (D2). A review task needs the model to flag SQL injection and authentication bypass in diffs. How should the criterion be written?

As testable criteria: name the exact vulnerability classes to flag. 'Be careful' is vague and untestable.

Q23 (D2). A team wants the cheapest correct setup for classifying 200,000 tickets a day into 12 categories. Tier?

Fast tier. High-volume, well-bounded classification is the Haiku-class tell; flagship here is flagship-everywhere.

Q24 (D7). Every engineer's Claude Code must enforce the same review conventions and reach the same internal MCP servers. Where does the config live?

Version-controlled project config: committed CLAUDE.md and project-scoped MCP config with environment-variable secrets. Personal configs depend on every individual complying forever.

Q25 (D7). The enterprise must guarantee no Claude Code session can ever call external network tools, on every repo, every machine, and separately wants coding standards applied everywhere. Which pairing?

The network ban in managed settings (permission deny rules, enforced by the client), the standards in the managed CLAUDE.md (guidance). Enforcement and guidance are different layers.

Pre-exam checklist

Why this comes last.

Recall proven. The last page before the exam: logistics, timing, and the final checks.

Run this list the night before. Every line should be a yes.

  • I can choose augmented LLM vs workflow vs agentic from a scenario, defaulting to the simplest sufficient pattern
  • I can name the four parts of a complete architecture, including the feedback loop
  • I can justify or refuse multi-agent decomposition
  • I can anchor recommendations to efficiency, cost, or performance SLA pillars
  • I can pick a model tier from capability, cost, and latency, and I know when routing beats one model
  • I know the cache economics and all three cache-breaking mistakes
  • I can select MCP vs direct API vs agent-to-agent from reuse and independence tells
  • I can spot capability bloat and explain progressive discovery
  • I know why per-user authorization beats shared service accounts
  • I can reason chunk-size trade-offs, I know the re-ranking trigger, and I fix retrieval before stuffing context
  • I can match metrics to failure modes and design a held-out, production-shaped eval set
  • I know the grader, judge, and human division of labor and how judge calibration works
  • I can run a clean one-variable experiment and diagnose failures from symptoms
  • I can list the five guardrail layers in order and place each attack or failure at the right layer
  • I know HITL placement rules and the non-triggers (sentiment, self-reported confidence)
  • I can distinguish GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP in one line each and match them to scenarios
  • I can name the six lifecycle phases in order and all five discovery buckets
  • I can structure an SLA for a probabilistic system with an error budget
  • I know what an ADR captures and when it is the answer
  • I know why team standards live in version-controlled project config
  • I know the managed-settings vs managed-CLAUDE.md split cold
  • I have the 25 trap patterns down and I apply them per option on multiple-response items
  • I read the question line first, I flag at 3 minutes, I save 10 minutes for review
